title: (Scenario) A critical production incident was just reported — what do you check FIRST, how do you assess the impact, and how do you prioritize restoring service before doing deep root-cause analysis? In simple steps: (1) FIRST confirm and size the impact; (2) look for WHAT CHANGED most recently; (3) MITIGATE FIRST to restore service; (4) keep communicating status; (5) only AFTER service is restored do the deep root-cause analysis. Why is "mitigate before root-cause" the rule, and why is rollback usually the fastest safe mitigation?
shortTitle: Critical production incident — what to check first, assess impact, prioritize restoring service, and why mitigate before root-cause

s1_definition.profdef: When a critical incident is reported, the disciplined response is to first confirm and size the real user impact using dashboards and user-facing signals, then look for what changed most recently because that is the most common and fastest-to-undo cause, then mitigate first to restore service by the fastest safe means such as a rollback, flag flip, scale-out, or failover, while continuously communicating status, and only after service is restored perform deep root-cause analysis and a blameless postmortem. Mitigate-before-root-cause is the rule because every minute of outage costs users and money, and you can investigate safely once the system is stable; rollback is usually the fastest safe mitigation because it returns the system to a known-good state.
s1_definition.analogy: If a critical alarm sounds at the National Bank of India, you do not first investigate who caused it. You first check how bad it really is and who it affects — are transfers down for everyone or is it a minor glitch? Then you ask what just changed, because a change we made minutes ago is usually the culprit and the quickest thing to undo. Then you stop the bleeding — most often by reverting to the version that worked an hour ago — while telling customers and managers what is going on. Only once everything is working again do you sit down to figure out exactly why it broke. The reason is simple: while money cannot move, every minute hurts customers, so restore first and investigate after.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a critical incident is reported, the disciplined response is to first confirm and size the real user impact using dashboards and user-facing signals, then look for what changed most recently because that is the most common and fastest-to-undo cause, then mitigate first to restore service by the fastest safe means such as a rollback, flag flip, scale-out, or failover, while continuously communicating status, and only after service is restored perform deep root-cause analysis and a blameless postmortem. Mitigate-before-root-cause is the rule because every minute of outage costs users and money, and you can investigate safely once the system is stable; rollback is usually the fastest safe mitigation because it returns the system to a known-good state.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** If a critical alarm sounds at the National Bank of India, you do not first investigate who caused it. You first check how bad it really is and who it affects — are transfers down for everyone or is it a minor glitch? Then you ask what just changed, because a change we made minutes ago is usually the culprit and the quickest thing to undo. Then you stop the bleeding — most often by reverting to the version that worked an hour ago — while telling customers and managers what is going on. Only once everything is working again do you sit down to figure out exactly why it broke. The reason is simple: while money cannot move, every minute hurts customers, so restore first and investigate after.

**One line to remember:** First confirm and size impact, then check what changed, then mitigate first — usually by rollback to a known-good state — while communicating, and do deep root-cause only after service is restored, because every minute of outage costs users and you can investigate safely once stable.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing to check is the actual user impact, not a single component's status. You open the dashboards and look at user-facing SLIs — error rate, latency, and successful-transaction rate — and you answer concrete questions: what exactly is broken, for how many users, in which regions or tenants, since when, and is it getting worse or stabilizing. The trap to avoid is declaring "the pod is up, so we are fine" when users are still failing; you trust the signals that reflect real customer experience. Sizing the impact this way both sets the severity and focuses the response on what matters.

The second step is to look for what changed most recently, because the overwhelming majority of incidents are triggered by a recent change — a deployment, a configuration or feature-flag change, an infrastructure change, or a sudden traffic shift — and a recent change is both the most likely cause and the fastest thing to undo. You check the deployment timeline, recent config and flag changes, and any dependency that started misbehaving, overlaying the incident start time on the change log. If the incident began at the exact moment of a deploy, you have your prime suspect without needing to understand the code yet.

The third step is to mitigate first to restore service, by the fastest safe means. The options are rolling back the last release, flipping a problematic feature flag off, scaling out to absorb load, failing over to a healthy region or replica, or shedding and rate-limiting load to protect the core. The goal here is explicitly not to understand everything — it is to stop the impact. Rollback is usually the fastest safe mitigation because it returns the system to a state that was known to be working, so it does not require diagnosing the new failure; you simply go back to what worked. This is why keeping the previous version warm and deployments reversible is so valuable. The fourth step, running in parallel, is to keep communicating status to stakeholders and customers on a regular cadence, because silence during an outage destroys trust faster than the outage itself, and clear communication also keeps responders coordinated.

The fifth step, only after service is restored, is deep root-cause analysis followed by a blameless postmortem. Now that the system is stable and users are no longer harmed, you can safely take the time to understand exactly why it failed — reproduce it, examine traces and logs, and identify the true cause — and then put in durable fixes and preventive action items. The reason mitigate-before-root-cause is the rule is twofold: first, outages have a direct, continuous cost in lost customer trust, failed transactions, and money, so the primary duty is to shorten the outage; second, investigating under the pressure of an active outage is slow and error-prone and can even make things worse, whereas investigating a stable system is calm, safe, and thorough. A senior nuance is that mitigation and root cause are genuinely different objectives that should not be conflated — a good responder resists the strong temptation to "just find the bug first" and instead restores service, because a faster restore is almost always achievable than a faster full diagnosis, and the diagnosis loses nothing by waiting until the system is safe.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India reports a critical incident: customers cannot complete transfers. We want an incident responder that executes the five steps in order — size impact, find what changed, mitigate first, communicate, then defer root-cause — and proves that mitigation (rollback) happens before any deep analysis.

Problem 1 — The team might panic and start reading code. The responder enforces checking impact and recent changes first.

Problem 2 — The team might try to fully diagnose before restoring service, prolonging the outage. The responder mitigates first via rollback and explicitly defers root-cause.

Problem 3 — Stakeholders need updates throughout. The responder posts status at each step. Our runnable Java simulation models an `IncidentResponder` that runs the ordered steps, choosing rollback as the fastest safe mitigation and recording that root-cause analysis is scheduled only after restoration. Classes: `ImpactAssessment`, `ChangeEvent`, `IncidentResponder`, and a `CriticalIncidentDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run the Java demo
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.critical.CriticalIncidentDemo

# Real first-5-minutes commands
# 1) impact: open Grafana SLO dashboard; check error rate + success rate by region
# 2) what changed: 
kubectl rollout history deployment/transfer-service
#    check recent config/flag changes + deploy timeline
# 3) mitigate FIRST:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/transfer-service      # rollback = fastest safe
# 4) comms: update status page every few minutes
# 5) root-cause AFTER restore: analyze traces/logs, write postmortem
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a critical incident report that customers cannot complete transfers.

Step 1 — Size impact: the responder reads user-facing signals and finds about twenty-two thousand customers across all of India affected, six minutes in and worsening, which is a SEV1. It immediately posts a status update that it is investigating.

Step 2 — What changed: the responder lists recent changes and picks the most recent one, a transfer-service deploy of version 6.0 seven minutes ago, as the prime suspect, noting it is reversible. The nightly batch and an older flag change are less likely because they are not the most recent.

Step 3 — Mitigate first: because the suspect change is reversible, the responder rolls it back to the known-good state, which begins restoring service, explicitly without doing any deep analysis yet — the rollback works because it returns to what worked, not because anyone understood the new bug.

Step 4 — Communicate: throughout, the responder posts updates — investigating, mitigation applied, and then service restored and being monitored — keeping stakeholders and customers informed on a steady cadence.

Step 5 — Root-cause after restore: only once service is stable does the responder begin calm, thorough root-cause analysis and schedule a blameless postmortem with preventive action items, because now the investigation can be done safely without the pressure of an active outage.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [SEVERE ] CRITICAL INCIDENT reported: customers cannot complete transfers
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [SEVERE ] [1 IMPACT] SEV1 — 22000 users in all-India, 6min in, worsening=true
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [INFO   ] [4 COMMS] status page + stakeholders: Investigating transfer failures affecting many customers (SEV1).
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [WARNING] [2 WHAT CHANGED] prime suspect: 'transfer-service deploy v6.0' 7min ago, reversible=true
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [INFO   ] [3 MITIGATE] ROLLBACK 'transfer-service deploy v6.0' → known-good state. Service restoring. (No root-cause needed yet.)
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [INFO   ] [4 COMMS] status page + stakeholders: Mitigation applied (rolled back recent deploy); service recovering.
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [INFO   ] [4 COMMS] status page + stakeholders: Service restored; monitoring for stability.
2026-10-30 03:15:00 [INFO   ] [5 ROOT CAUSE] service stable → now safe to investigate calmly + write blameless postmortem with preventive action items.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a critical production incident is reported, the first thing I check is the actual user impact, not a single component's status. I open the dashboards and look at user-facing signals — error rate, latency, and successful-transaction rate — to answer concrete questions: what exactly is broken, for how many users, in which regions, since when, and whether it is getting worse. I avoid the trap of saying "the pod is up, so we are fine" when customers are still failing, because the signals that matter are the ones reflecting real customer experience, and sizing impact this way sets the severity and focuses the whole response.

The second step is to look for what changed most recently, because the overwhelming majority of incidents are triggered by a recent change — a deploy, a config or feature-flag change, an infrastructure change, or a traffic shift — and a recent change is both the most likely cause and the fastest thing to undo. So I overlay the incident start time on the change log, and if it began at the exact moment of a deploy, I have my prime suspect without needing to understand the code yet. The third step is to mitigate first to restore service by the fastest safe means — rolling back the last release, flipping a feature flag off, scaling out, failing over, or shedding load — and the goal here is explicitly not to understand everything, it is to stop the impact. Rollback is usually the fastest safe mitigation because it returns the system to a state that was known to be working, so it does not require diagnosing the new failure; I simply go back to what worked, which is why keeping the previous version warm and deployments reversible is so valuable. Running in parallel, the fourth step is to keep communicating status on a steady cadence, because silence during an outage destroys trust faster than the outage itself.

Only after service is restored, as the fifth step, do I do deep root-cause analysis and a blameless postmortem, because now the system is stable and I can investigate calmly and thoroughly without harming users. The reason mitigate-before-root-cause is the rule is twofold: outages have a direct, continuous cost in failed transactions, lost trust, and money, so my primary duty is to shorten the outage; and investigating under the pressure of a live outage is slow, error-prone, and can make things worse, whereas investigating a stable system is safe and thorough. In my project at the National Bank of India, when customers suddenly could not complete transfers, I sized the impact as a SEV1 affecting tens of thousands, identified a deploy from minutes earlier as the prime suspect, rolled it back to restore service before doing any deep analysis, communicated throughout, and only then investigated and wrote the postmortem. The senior point I always make is that mitigation and root cause are different objectives that must not be conflated — a faster restore is almost always achievable than a faster full diagnosis, and the diagnosis loses nothing by waiting until the system is safe.
